topics.title: Tu or vous? How formal to be in France
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about how people address each other in France. This is habit, not law: it varies by region, age, workplace and person, so listen to how others speak.
topics.intro: French has two words for you when you speak to one person: tu and vous. Tu is for friends, family, children and people close to you. Vous is for strangers, for people you want to show respect to, and in formal situations. Vous is also the plural, so it is how you speak to several people.
topics.question: Est-ce qu'il y a une forme polie de « you » dans votre langue ? (Does your language have a polite form of "you"?)
facts: Use tu with friends, family, children and, often, people of your own age in a relaxed setting.
Use vous with strangers, in shops, at the préfecture, with a doctor or a landlord you do not know, and whenever you want to show respect.
The verb changes: with tu you say Comment vas-tu ? or Ça va ? and with vous you say Comment allez-vous ?
Vous is also the plural. To a group of friends you say vous as well: Vous venez à la soirée ?

At work it depends on the company: many teams use tu between colleagues, others keep vous with managers or clients. Listen to what the others say. In Québec, tu is more common in everyday situations than in France.
Not sure? Start with vous and wait. Often the other person says: On se tutoie ? or Tu peux me tutoyer (You can use tu with me).

topics.title: Greetings: bonjour first, la bise, the handshake
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about greetings in France. These are habits, not rules: they change with region, age, setting and person. When in doubt, watch what the others do.
topics.intro: In France, greeting people is part of every exchange. You say bonjour when you walk into a shop, a waiting room or a lift, before you ask for anything. Between friends people often do la bise, and in formal settings a handshake is usual.
topics.question: Comment est-ce qu'on se salue dans votre pays ? (How do people greet each other in your country?)
facts: Say Bonjour (Madame / Monsieur) when you enter a shop, a café or a doctor's waiting room. Starting with your request alone can sound rude.
In the evening many people switch to Bonsoir. Salut is informal, for friends and people your age.

La bise is a light kiss on the cheek, or a cheek-to-cheek touch. It is common between friends and family and, in many workplaces, between colleagues who know each other well. The number of bises (two, three or four) varies by region.
At a first meeting at work, with a boss or a client, a handshake (une poignée de main) is the safe choice. Some people prefer no contact at all: follow their lead.
When you leave a shop, say Merci, au revoir, bonne journée. Saying au revoir to the whole waiting room is also common practice.
In Québec, bonjour is also often heard as a goodbye, and la bise is less common than in France.

topics.title: Daily rhythm: meal times, opening hours, Sundays
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about daily life in France, as of 2026. Opening hours and Sunday work depend on the shop, the town and the type of business: check the hours of the place itself. See service-public.fr for the rules on Sunday work.
topics.intro: The French day follows a common rhythm: breakfast, lunch around noon, dinner in the evening. Many small shops close at lunchtime or on Sunday and Monday, and many offices keep fixed hours, so it helps to know when things are open.
topics.question: À quelle heure est-ce que vous mangez ? (What time do you eat?)
facts: Lunch (le déjeuner) is usually between noon and 2 p.m. Dinner (le dîner) is often around 7:30 to 9 p.m. Many restaurants serve lunch only until about 2 p.m.
In many towns, small shops, bakeries and doctors' surgeries close for a break around lunchtime, and some close on Monday. Big supermarkets are often open all day.
On Sunday, most shops are closed. Bakeries, many food shops and markets are open in the morning, and shops in tourist areas may be open all day. The rules are detailed and have exceptions.
Public offices (mairie, préfecture, CAF) are usually open on weekdays only and may close early on some days. Check the hours online before you go.
Le goûter is a snack around 4 p.m., mainly for children. L'apéro (apéritif) is a drink with snacks before dinner, usually with friends or family.
Pharmacies take turns to stay open at night and on Sunday (pharmacie de garde). The sign on a pharmacy's door shows the nearest one.

topics.title: Cafés, service compris and l'addition
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about cafés, restaurants and tipping in France, as of 2026. Tipping is a custom, not a rule. Prices on the menu include service (see service-public.fr and the economie.gouv.fr pages on restaurants).
topics.intro: In French cafés and restaurants, the price on the menu already includes service: the words service compris mean that. A tip (un pourboire) is a small extra, not an obligation. It helps to know what to order and how to ask for the bill.
topics.question: Est-ce qu'on laisse un pourboire dans votre pays ? (Do people leave a tip in your country?)
facts: Prices in cafés and restaurants include service by law. A tip is optional: many people leave some small change, or a euro or two for good service, but nobody expects a percentage.
Un café means a small, strong black coffee (an espresso). For milk, ask for un café crème or un noisette (espresso with a drop of milk). Un allongé is a longer coffee.
Tap water is free in restaurants: ask for une carafe d'eau. A bottle of water is charged.
At a café, a drink at the bar (au comptoir) is often cheaper than at a table or on the terrace. The menu or a sign shows both prices.

You usually pay at the end. Call the waiter with Monsieur / Madame, s'il vous plaît, and ask L'addition, s'il vous plaît. Most places accept cards and contactless payment, but a small café may have a minimum amount.
In Québec, tipping is expected and the tip is usually around 15 percent: service is not included in the price.

topics.title: Regions, departments and overseas France
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about the administrative map of France, as of 2026. Names, boundaries and powers can change. Official sources: service-public.fr, interieur.gouv.fr, insee.fr and vie-publique.fr.
topics.intro: Mainland France is divided into 13 regions, including Corsica. Each region is made up of departments, and each department has a number you see in postcodes and on old number plates. Overseas France has more regions and departments.
topics.question: Dans quelle région habitez-vous ? (Which region do you live in?)
facts: There are 13 regions in mainland France, including Corsica (Corse). Since 2016 there are fewer than before, when there were 22: some regions were merged.
Overseas, there are five regions, also overseas departments (les DROM): Guadeloupe, Martinique, Guyane (French Guiana), La Réunion and Mayotte. Other overseas territories have a different status.

Departments are often counted as 101 in total: 96 in mainland France and 5 overseas. Corsica's two departments, 2A and 2B, are still used in numbers and postcodes, although Corsica has had a single local authority since 2018.
The first two digits of a postcode are usually the department number: 75 is Paris, 13 is Bouches-du-Rhône, 59 is Nord. Overseas departments start with 97, for example 974 for La Réunion.

Each region has a main city that hosts the regional council (le conseil régional). Regions manage things like regional trains, lycées and economic development. The préfet represents the State in each department.
Many people say the name of their department when they say where they live: Je suis du 33 means I am from the Gironde.

topics.title: Public holidays and le pont
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about public holidays (jours fériés) in France, as of 2026. Rules on working on a holiday depend on your contract and collective agreement. Official source: service-public.fr (jours fériés).
topics.intro: France has 11 national public holidays (jours fériés). Some have a fixed date, and others depend on the date of Easter. When a holiday falls close to a weekend, many people take a day off to make a long weekend: this is called faire le pont.
topics.question: Quels jours sont fériés dans votre pays ? (Which days are public holidays in your country?)
facts: The 11 jours fériés are: 1 January, Easter Monday, 1 May, 8 May, Ascension, Whit Monday, 14 July, 15 August, 1 November, 11 November and 25 December.
Easter Monday, Ascension and Whit Monday move every year with Easter. Ascension is always a Thursday, and the other two are Mondays.

1 May (Fête du Travail) is the one holiday that the law generally makes a paid day off for everyone, with few exceptions. For the other holidays, whether you work depends on your contract and your sector.

Le pont means taking one extra day off between a holiday and the weekend, for example the Friday after Ascension. It is not an official holiday: ask your employer. The journée de solidarité is a different thing: one working day a year for which employees are not paid, which many employers place on Whit Monday, but it is not always so.
In Alsace and in the Moselle département, two more days are public holidays: Good Friday (Vendredi saint) and 26 December (Saint-Étienne).
When a holiday falls on a Saturday or Sunday, you do not get a day in exchange by law. Check your own contract.

topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about meals and food words in France, as of 2026. Habits change with region, family and age. For the official rules on bread and on labels, see economie.gouv.fr.
topics.intro: Meals are a fixed part of the French day: breakfast, lunch, dinner, and often a snack for children. Many people shop for fresh bread every day, and cheese and bread are on most tables. Some words are used differently in France and in Québec.
topics.question: Quel est votre plat préféré ? (What is your favourite dish?)
facts: In France, le petit-déjeuner is breakfast, le déjeuner is lunch and le dîner is dinner. In Québec, déjeuner is breakfast, dîner is lunch and souper is dinner.
A traditional meal has several courses: an entrée (starter), a plat (main course), cheese, and a dessert. Many families eat a simpler version on weekdays.
A baguette is a long loaf of white bread, often bought fresh every day at the boulangerie. A baguette tradition is made with a specific recipe. For a small loaf, ask for une ficelle or un pain.
Many restaurants offer a menu du jour or une formule at lunchtime: a set meal (for example plat + dessert, or entrée + plat) at a fixed price. It is usually cheaper than ordering à la carte.
Fromage is served before dessert, or with bread. There are many cheeses: for example camembert, comté, roquefort and chèvre. Ask: Qu'est-ce que vous me conseillez ?
Ask about allergies or diet in the restaurant: Je suis végétarien(ne) is understood, but some kitchens use meat stock, so ask what is in the dish.

topics.title: Festivals: 14 juillet, Fête de la musique and more
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about festivals in France, as of 2026. Dates and programmes change each year: check the website of the mairie or the tourist office before you go.
topics.intro: France has national celebrations, seasonal traditions and local festivals. Some are public holidays, and some are only customs. Many involve food: crêpes, galettes, a long family dinner.
topics.question: Quelle fête aimez-vous le plus ? (Which festival do you like most?)
facts: On 14 July, the Fête nationale, there is a military parade in Paris in the morning and fireworks in the evening in many towns. Many towns hold a bal in the evening.
The Fête de la musique takes place every year on 21 June, the summer solstice. Amateurs and professionals play music in streets, squares and bars, and the concerts are mostly free.

La Chandeleur on 2 February is the day of the crêpes. A galette des rois is eaten in early January for Epiphany: the person who finds the fève (a small charm hidden in the cake) is king or queen for the day.
Carnival is held in late winter in several places, for example in Nice and Dunkerque, and in overseas France in Guyane, Martinique and Guadeloupe.
The Nuit blanche is a night in autumn when museums and public places are open all night with art events; it began in Paris and now exists in other cities. The date is set every year.
For Noël, many people have a big dinner on 24 December, the réveillon, and a meal with the family on 25 December. The Beaujolais nouveau, a young wine, is released on the third Thursday in November.

topics.title: Recycling: bac jaune, glass, compost, déchetterie
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about waste sorting in France, as of 2026. The rules, the colours of the bins and the collection days are set by your commune or intercommunalité, so they differ from place to place. Check the website of your mairie, and see ecologie.gouv.fr and consignesdetri.fr.
topics.intro: In France, sorting waste (le tri) is common, but the system changes from town to town. The colour of the bins, what goes where and the collection days depend on where you live. Always check the rules of your commune.
topics.question: Est-ce que vous triez vos déchets ? (Do you sort your waste?)
facts: The bac jaune (yellow bin) is usually for packaging and paper. In recent years, most communes accept all plastic packaging in it; some still have local rules.
Glass (le verre) usually goes in a separate container, often a green column (une borne à verre) in the street. Bottles and jars go in without the lids.
The other household waste (ordures ménagères) goes in another bin, often grey or green. Collection days are set by your commune: look at the leaflet, the website or a sticker on the bin.

Food waste (biodéchets) can go in a composteur, a compost bin in the garden or shared in a building, or in a special bin if your commune offers one. Sorting food waste is being extended across France: ask your mairie what exists locally.

The déchetterie is a recycling centre outside town. You bring large items (encombrants), electronics, old furniture, garden waste and hazardous waste there, usually free for residents. You may need a badge or proof of address.
In a block of flats, the bins are usually in the courtyard or the cellar area. If you rent, ask your landlord or the gardien where they are.

Procedures differ by préfecture, mairie and office: always follow the instructions of the office or its official website. See service-public.fr, ameli.fr and the ANEF site for foreigners' procedures.
topics.intro: In France, many services work by rendez-vous. You book a time with a doctor, a mairie or a préfecture, often online, and you are expected to come on time. A rendez-vous can also be a meeting with friends.
topics.question: Comment est-ce que vous prenez rendez-vous ? (How do you make an appointment?)
facts: For doctors, dentists and other health professionals, many people book on Doctolib, a booking website and app. Some practices use another system, or only the phone.

Many mairies and préfectures offer online booking on their own websites. For some residence permit procedures, you start in your ANEF account, and the préfecture may send you an appointment or a convocation by email. The details depend on your case and your préfecture.
Bring the confirmation (convocation) and your original documents. The office tells you what to bring: read the message carefully.
If you cannot come, cancel or move the appointment, by the link in the email or by phone. A missed slot can mean a long wait for the next one.
For a doctor, an office or a work meeting, be on time or a few minutes early. For a dinner at a friend's home, many people arrive a little after the time, but not for an official appointment.
The wait for an appointment can be long, especially for specialists or in some préfectures. Try again later, check for cancelled slots, or ask the office if there is another way.

topics.title: Proving your address: the justificatif de domicile
topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on the practical sheets of service-public.fr (justificatif de domicile, attestation d'hébergement, changement d'adresse). Accepted documents differ by office and by procedure, so always check what the office asks for (as of 2026).
topics.intro: In France you do not register your address with the town hall when you move in. Instead, you prove where you live, again and again, with a justificatif de domicile. Banks, the préfecture, the CAF and schools all ask for one.
topics.question: Faut-il déclarer son adresse dans votre pays ? (Do you have to register your address in your home country?)
facts: There is no general residence registration in France. Nobody gives you a certificate when you move in. What counts is a document with your name and your address on it.

A justificatif de domicile is usually a recent bill: electricity, gas, water or a landline or internet contract. A quittance de loyer (rent receipt) or an avis d'imposition (tax notice) also works at many offices.
Offices often want a document that is less than three months old, but this changes from one office to another. Some do not accept every kind of bill, so ask which documents they take.

If you stay with somebody and nothing is in your name, your host can write an attestation d'hébergement. It is a signed statement that you live with them. Offices usually also want a copy of the host's ID and a justificatif de domicile in the host's name.

Your mairie (town hall) does not register you, but you deal with it for school enrolment, civil-status documents (acte de naissance, acte de mariage) and, if you are entitled to vote, the electoral roll.

When you move, you have to tell many bodies about your new address: your bank, your employer, the CAF, the tax office, insurers. An online service on service-public.fr lets you notify several of them at once. Check which ones it covers.

topics.sourceNote: General orientation from ameli.fr (the Assurance Maladie site) and service-public.fr. Who is covered, which scheme applies and how much is reimbursed depends on your situation, so check ameli.fr or ask your caisse (as of 2026).
topics.intro: In France the Assurance Maladie reimburses part of your health costs. You usually pay the doctor first and get money back afterwards. Many people also have a mutuelle, a complementary insurance, for the rest.
topics.question: Comment ça se passe chez le médecin dans votre pays ? (How does going to the doctor work in your country?)
facts: People who work in France are covered through the Assurance Maladie. People who live in France in a stable way and are not covered through work can usually be covered under the general scheme often called PUMA. The conditions depend on your situation, so check ameli.fr.

Your first step is usually to get a social security number and to open an account on ameli.fr. The Assurance Maladie then gives you the carte Vitale, a card with a chip (also available as an app). You show it at the doctor, the pharmacy and the hospital.

Choose a médecin traitant (a family doctor) and declare him or her to the Assurance Maladie. This is part of the parcours de soins coordonné: you usually see your médecin traitant first, and he or she sends you to a specialist if needed. Outside this path you are usually reimbursed less.

The Assurance Maladie reimburses a part of the price of a visit, tests and medicine. The rest is for you or for your mutuelle. People on a low income may get help with this part, for example through a scheme called the CSS (complémentaire santé solidaire). Check the conditions on ameli.fr.
A mutuelle is an optional complementary insurance. Many employers offer one to their employees. Compare the cover before you choose.

In an emergency call 15 (SAMU, medical emergencies), 18 (pompiers, fire brigade), 17 (police) or 112, the European emergency number. The urgences of a hospital treat serious cases. For smaller problems, ask at a pharmacie (green cross). At night and on Sundays, a pharmacie de garde stays open.

topics.title: Renting a flat: bail, dépôt de garantie, état des lieux, charges
topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on the practical sheets of service-public.fr on renting (bail, dépôt de garantie, état des lieux, préavis) and on caf.fr (APL). Rules differ for unfurnished and furnished flats and in some areas, and they are amended from time to time. Read your own bail and check the current rules (as of 2026).
topics.intro: A rented home in France is covered by law, which sets minimum tenant rights, and by your bail (the lease). Read the bail before you sign, and keep every paper: the état des lieux, the rent receipts, the insurance.
topics.question: Comment loue-t-on un logement dans votre pays ? (How do people rent a home in your country?)
facts: The bail is the rental contract. For an empty (unfurnished) flat it usually runs for three years, for a furnished one (meublé) usually for one year. Check the exact rules for your case.

The dépôt de garantie is a deposit that the landlord keeps until you leave. The law limits it: for an unfurnished flat it is usually one month's rent without charges, for a furnished one it can be higher. The landlord has to give it back by a legal deadline, minus costs he or she can justify.

The état des lieux is a written check of the condition of the flat, made with the landlord when you move in and again when you leave. Note every defect, take photos and keep your copy. The two documents are compared at the end.

The loyer is the rent. The charges are costs on top (heating, water, the cleaning of shared parts). Ask if the rent is « charges comprises » or « hors charges ». Electricity, gas and internet are often separate contracts in your name.

A tenant has to take out an assurance habitation (home insurance) and show it to the landlord. To leave, you give préavis (notice), usually by a registered letter. It is often three months for an unfurnished flat and one month for a furnished one, but there are exceptions.
The APL (aide personnalisée au logement) is a housing benefit paid by the CAF. It depends on your income, your rent and your situation. You can test your case on caf.fr.

Landlords often ask for a garant (a person who guarantees your rent). Visale is a free guarantee offered by Action Logement for some tenants under conditions. The law limits which documents a landlord can ask for, so you do not have to hand over everything.

topics.title: The school system: maternelle, élémentaire, collège, lycée
topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on education.gouv.fr and service-public.fr (scolarité, inscription à l'école, baccalauréat). Enrolment steps, canteen prices and extra-school services are set by each commune, so ask your mairie and the school (as of 2026).
topics.intro: School in France is compulsory from age 3 to 16. It follows a fixed path: maternelle, école élémentaire, collège, then lycée, which ends with the baccalauréat (le bac). The school year starts in early September, with the rentrée.
topics.question: À quel âge commence l'école dans votre pays ? (At what age does school start in your country?)
facts: As of 2026, schooling is compulsory from age 3 to 16. The école maternelle (ages 3 to 6) is therefore part of it. Public school is free.
The école élémentaire lasts five years, from about 6 to 11. The classes are called CP, CE1, CE2, CM1 and CM2.
The collège lasts four years, from about 11 to 15. The classes are counted backwards: sixième, cinquième, quatrième, troisième. At the end students take the brevet.

The lycée lasts three years, from about 15 to 18: seconde, première, terminale. There are lycées généraux et technologiques and lycées professionnels. At the end, students take the baccalauréat (le bac), which is also the first university diploma.
Marks are given out of 20. Ten is a pass. A 16 is a very good mark, and teachers rarely give 20.

Many schools have a cantine (canteen). It is often run by the commune, and the price often depends on the family situation. There are also services before and after class (périscolaire). Ask your mairie.

For a first enrolment in primary school you usually start at the mairie and then register with the school's head. You often need ID, a family document or birth certificate, proof of address and proof of vaccinations. If your child does not speak French yet, ask the school about help for newly arrived pupils.

topics.title: Finding a job: France Travail, CV, CDI and CDD
topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on francetravail.fr (formerly Pôle emploi) and service-public.fr (contrat de travail, CDI, CDD, intérim). Whether you may work depends on your nationality and permit. Check the official pages for your case (as of 2026).
topics.intro: To look for work in France you can register with France Travail, use job websites, apply directly to companies and ask your contacts. First check that your permit allows you to work, then learn the main contract types: CDI, CDD and intérim.
topics.question: Comment cherche-t-on du travail dans votre pays ? (How do people look for work in your country?)
facts: Citizens of non-EU countries usually need a permit that allows them to work. The rules depend on your nationality and situation, so ask the préfecture or look at service-public.fr.

France Travail is the public employment service. Until 2024 it was called Pôle emploi, and you will still hear the old name. You register online as demandeur d'emploi (job seeker) on francetravail.fr, and an adviser follows your case.

A French CV is usually one or two pages: contact details, experience, studies, languages. Many employers also ask for a lettre de motivation, a short letter that says why you want this job. Adapt it to each offer. A photo is not required.

A CDI (contrat à durée indéterminée) has no end date. It is the usual contract. A CDD (contrat à durée déterminée) has an end date and is allowed only for certain reasons, for example a replacement. At the end of a CDD you often get an extra payment, the prime de précarité, with exceptions.
Intérim (temping) means that an agence d'intérim employs you and sends you on missions to companies. Apprentissage and alternance combine a job with studies and are paid.

A CDI often starts with a période d'essai (trial period). Always ask for the contract in writing and check the type, the working hours, the convention collective (collective agreement) and the salary. Salaries are often quoted brut (before deductions), and the net is what you receive.

topics.sourceNote: Based on the Constitution of 1958 (articles 2 and 75-1, legifrance.gouv.fr) and on the pages of the Ministry of Culture on the languages of France (culture.gouv.fr). The place of regional languages in schools and public life is debated and set by laws and local decisions, so ask locally (as of 2026).
topics.intro: France has one official language: French. Yet other languages are spoken in the regions and overseas, and you will see them on signs and hear them in some places. They are part of the country's heritage, but they have no official status.
topics.question: Quelles langues parle-t-on dans votre région ? (Which languages are spoken in your region?)
facts: The Constitution says: « La langue de la République est le français. » French is the language of administration, the courts and public schools. There is no co-official language at national level.
Another article of the Constitution says that regional languages belong to the heritage of France. So they are recognised and protected in principle, but without official status.

Breton is spoken in Brittany, Occitan in much of the south, Alsatian (a Germanic dialect) in Alsace, Corsican in Corsica, Basque in the Pays basque, and Catalan in the Roussillon, near the Spanish border.

Overseas, many people speak créoles (in Guadeloupe, Martinique, Guyane and La Réunion), and there are Polynesian and Kanak languages in Polynesia and New Caledonia. Many speak both French and the local language.

In schools, a regional language may be offered as an option, in bilingual classes, or in immersion schools. Some of these schools are run by associations, for example Diwan for Breton and the ikastolak for Basque. The offer differs by region, so ask the school or the académie.
You will see bilingual street signs and place names in some regions. You can live anywhere in France using French only, but a few words of the local language are often much appreciated.

topics.title: French in the world: one language, many varieties
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about where French is official or widely used, based on the pages of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (francophonie.org), the Office québécois de la langue française (oqlf.gouv.qc.ca) and the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Status and figures differ by source and change over time, so treat them as approximate (as of 2026).
topics.intro: French is an official language in many countries on several continents, from Belgium and Switzerland to Québec, West and Central Africa and the Caribbean. It is one language with many varieties, and speakers understand each other well.
topics.question: Quels mots français connaissez-vous d'autres pays ? (Which French words do you know from other countries?)
facts: In Europe, French is official in France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg and Monaco. In Canada, it is the official language of Québec, and it is also official at the federal level.

In Africa, French is official or widely used in many countries, for example Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon and the DR Congo, often next to local languages. In the Maghreb (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia), French is not the main official language but is widely used in education, business and media.
In the Caribbean, French is official in Guadeloupe and Martinique, which are part of France, and in Haiti, together with Haitian Creole. A large and growing share of French speakers lives in Africa.
The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) brings together many states and governments that share French as a language or have links with it.
In Belgium and in parts of Switzerland, people say septante (70) and nonante (90) instead of soixante-dix and quatre-vingt-dix. In some Swiss cantons you also hear huitante (80).

In Québec, the meals are called déjeuner (breakfast), dîner (lunch) and souper (the evening meal). The same use is common in Belgium and Switzerland. In France the evening meal is le dîner and the midday meal is le déjeuner.

Québec also has its own words: courriel (email), char (car, informal), magasiner (to go shopping), fin de semaine (weekend). People often say bienvenue for « you're welcome ». Québec has a special office, the OQLF, for French vocabulary.

These differences do not make one French right and another wrong. They are normal varieties of one language. In France, standard French is the reference for the exams and for forms, but you will meet many accents.

topics.title: Training and university: apprentissage, BTS, licence, recognising degrees
topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on service-public.fr, parcoursup.gouv.fr, enseignementsup-recherche.gouv.fr and the ENIC-NARIC France pages of France Education international (france-education-international.fr). Entry rules, fees, deadlines and procedures change and differ by programme and by country of origin, so check the official page before you apply (as of 2026).
topics.intro: After the bac or the collège, France offers vocational routes (CAP, bac pro, BTS, apprentissage) and the university. If you studied abroad, there are several different ways to have your qualification recognised, and it matters which one you ask for.
topics.question: Qu'avez-vous étudié et à quoi voulez-vous l'utiliser en France ? (What have you studied and what do you want to use it for in France?)
facts: The CAP (certificat d'aptitude professionnelle) is a vocational diploma for a trade, usually after two years of study. The BTS (brevet de technicien supérieur) lasts two years after the bac. The BUT (bachelor universitaire de technologie) lasts three years at a university institute.

Apprentissage and alternance mean that you alternate between a school (often a CFA, a centre de formation d'apprentis) and a company. You have a work contract and a salary. The contract types and age limits depend on the case, so check on service-public.fr.

At university the system is called LMD: licence (three years, bac +3), master (two more years, bac +5) and doctorat (three years). Alongside the universities there are the grandes écoles, often with classes préparatoires and an entrance competition (concours).

Parcoursup is the national online platform where most bac candidates apply for first-year places in higher education. In general terms: you enter your choices (vœux) in winter and spring, and the answers arrive in spring and summer. Applicants who live abroad outside Europe often use a different procedure, so check the official pages.

Public universities charge registration fees set by the state, which are relatively low. Fees can differ for some non-EU students, so ask the university. Entry to many private schools is more expensive.

Foreign diplomas: ENIC-NARIC France can issue an attestation de comparabilité, which states how your diploma compares with the French system. It is an opinion on the level, not an automatic equivalence, and it does not give a right to practise a profession. Each university or school decides on its own whether to admit you.

Regulated professions (for example doctor, lawyer, teacher, architect) have their own procedures with the professional body or the ministry concerned. Offices often ask for a traduction assermentée (a translation by a sworn translator). If you have work experience, the VAE (validation des acquis de l'expérience) can lead to a diploma. The processes can take months, so start early.

topics.title: Leaving a job: démission, rupture conventionnelle, licenciement
topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on the Code du travail (legifrance.gouv.fr), service-public.fr (démission, rupture conventionnelle, licenciement, solde de tout compte) and francetravail.fr on unemployment benefit. Conditions, amounts and deadlines change, and your contract or convention collective can differ. This is not legal advice: ask a union, a lawyer or France Travail (as of 2026).
topics.intro: When you leave a job in France, the way the contract ends decides what you are owed and whether you can claim unemployment benefit. Read your contract and your convention collective before you sign anything.
topics.question: Comment se termine un contrat de travail dans votre pays ? (How does an employment contract end in your country?)
facts: With a démission (resignation) the employee decides to leave. Say it clearly, and put it in writing (a short letter, by registered letter or handed over against a receipt). You normally work through a préavis, a notice period. Its length comes from your contract, your convention collective or the law.

A rupture conventionnelle is an end of the contract agreed between you and your employer. There is a negotiation, a signed agreement, a period during which each side can change its mind, and then the administration has to validate it. It usually gives a leaving payment, and it often opens the right to chômage if you meet the other conditions.

A licenciement (dismissal) is the employer's decision. It must have a real and serious reason. The employer has to follow a procedure: an invitation to an entretien préalable, then a letter of dismissal that states the reasons. It can be for personal reasons or for economic reasons.
Deadlines to challenge a dismissal are short, in front of the conseil de prud'hommes (labour court). Do not wait. A union, a lawyer or the services of the labour inspectorate can advise you.

At the end of the contract your employer has to give you three documents: a certificat de travail (the dates and the jobs you did), a reçu pour solde de tout compte (a statement of what you are paid at the end) and an attestation destinée à France Travail. Read the solde de tout compte carefully, and ask questions before you sign.

Chômage is paid as the ARE (allocation d'aide au retour à l'emploi) by France Travail. In general terms you need to have worked enough and to have lost your job involuntarily, and you register as a job seeker. A normal resignation usually gives no ARE, with exceptions. Check the conditions on francetravail.fr.

topics.intro: France has a family of public media: France Télévisions for television, Radio France for radio, plus Arte, TV5 Monde and RFI. They are a good source of real French for learners, and the way they are funded is a live public debate.
topics.question: Pensez-vous que tout le monde devrait financer un audiovisuel public ? Pourquoi ? (Do you think everyone should pay for public broadcasting? Why?)
facts: France Télévisions runs the channels France 2, France 3 (with regional editions), France 5 and the news channel franceinfo, and the streaming platform France.tv.
Radio France runs France Inter (general), franceinfo (news), France Culture (talks and culture), France Musique, FIP and the local network ici (formerly France Bleu).
Arte is a European cultural channel run jointly by France and Germany. Its programmes are shown in French and German, and online you can often choose subtitles.

TV5 Monde is an international French-language channel supported by several French-speaking countries. RFI (Radio France Internationale) is an international radio station. Both have material for learners, such as RFI's news in simple French.

The old television licence fee (la redevance audiovisuelle) was abolished in 2022. Public broadcasters are now financed mainly from the state budget, through a share of national VAT revenue. Check the current rules on service-public.fr.
The regulator Arcom chooses the heads of France Télévisions and Radio France. The way public media are funded and run has been discussed and changed more than once.

topics.title: Associations: the 1901 law and volunteering
topics.sourceNote: Based on the public guides on associations at service-public.fr and associations.gouv.fr, and on the law of 1 July 1901 (legifrance.gouv.fr), as of 2026. Founding steps, fees and volunteer rules differ by association, so ask the association or your mairie, and check the official sites before you act.
topics.intro: In France, many people belong to an association: a sports club, a parents' group, a choir, a charity. It is one of the easiest ways to meet people and to practise French in a relaxed setting, and living in France is usually all you need to join.
topics.question: Est-ce que tu fais partie d'une association ou d'un groupe dans ton pays ? (Do you belong to an association or a group in your country?)
facts: Associations are governed by the law of 1 July 1901. An association is a non-profit group: it can run activities and collect membership fees, but it does not share profits among its members.

To exist legally, an association is declared at the préfecture or sous-préfecture (this can be done online), and its creation is published in the Journal officiel des associations. The founders write the statuts, the rules of the group. At least two people are needed.

Members are called adhérents. They usually pay a cotisation (a yearly fee) and vote at the assemblée générale. They elect the conseil d'administration and the bureau: a président, a secrétaire and a trésorier.

Foreigners can generally join associations in France without special permission, so a club or a neighbourhood group is a good first community. Rules for leading an association can depend on its type, so ask.

In early September, most towns hold a forum des associations, often in a sports hall or a park: dozens of stands where you can ask about activities, prices and times, and sign up on the spot. Many sports and arts clubs start their year then.

Bénévolat (volunteering) is unpaid. Well-known organisations include the Restos du Cœur, the Secours populaire, the Croix-Rouge française and the Secours catholique, and there are many local groups for aid, tutoring or the environment. Ask what the tasks are, how much time it takes and whether the association insures its volunteers.

topics.intro: French is spoken on several continents, and each place has its own festivals, music and food. In France you will meet people from Québec, the Caribbean, West Africa and the Maghreb, so it helps to know which tradition comes from where.
topics.question: Quelle fête ou quel plat de ton pays voudrais-tu présenter à la classe ? (Which festival or dish from your country would you like to present to the class?)
facts: In Québec, the Fête nationale is on 24 June, also called la Saint-Jean. There are concerts, fireworks and bonfires across the province. In late winter and early spring, many families visit a cabane à sucre (a sugar shack) for meals with maple syrup.

Poutine is a Québec dish: chips with cheese curds and hot gravy. In Québec French the meals have different names: déjeuner is breakfast, dîner is lunch and souper is dinner. In France, déjeuner is lunch and dîner is dinner.
Guadeloupe and Martinique are part of France, as départements d'outre-mer. Their Carnaval usually runs from January until the days before Lent, with parades, costumes and music groups.
Zouk is a dance music from Guadeloupe and Martinique that became famous in the 1980s, with bands such as Kassav'. The gwoka is the drum music and dance of Guadeloupe, listed by UNESCO in 2014.

In West African countries such as Senegal, Mali and Côte d'Ivoire, French is often used next to other languages. Dishes known in France include thiéboudienne (rice with fish, from Senegal), mafé (a peanut stew, from Mali and Senegal) and attiéké (cassava semolina, from Côte d'Ivoire). Many families celebrate Tabaski (Eid al-Adha) together.

From Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia come couscous, which UNESCO listed in 2020 as shared heritage of four countries (these three and Mauritania), and mint tea. Ramadan and the Aïd are important for many families in France. Customs differ by country and by family.

topics.title: The State and decentralisation: from the préfet to the maire
topics.sourceNote: Based on the Constitution (articles 1, 72, 73; legifrance.gouv.fr) and on vie-publique.fr and collectivites-locales.gouv.fr, as of 2026. The number of communes changes a little every year, and which body handles what can differ locally, so check the site of your mairie, département or région.
topics.intro: France is a unitary State with several levels of local government. Each level has its own tasks. Knowing which level handles what tells you where to go for a school place, a residence permit, a bin collection or a social benefit.
topics.question: Qui s'occupe de quoi dans ton pays : la commune, la région ou l'État ? (Who handles what in your country: the municipality, the region or the State?)
facts: France is a unitary State, so laws are national. Since the 1980s, decentralisation has given more tasks to local authorities (collectivités territoriales): communes, départements and régions. Since 2003 the Constitution says that the organisation of the Republic is decentralised.

Metropolitan France has 13 régions, and five more are overseas (Guadeloupe, Martinique, Guyane, La Réunion, Mayotte), so 18 in total as of 2026. There are 101 départements, each with a number: 75 is Paris and 13 is Bouches-du-Rhône. The number is also the start of the postcode.

The préfet represents the State in each département, and a préfet de région does so in each région. The préfecture deals with residence permits (requests are now mostly made online), association declarations and public order, and it checks that local decisions respect the law.

The commune is the smallest level: there are around 35,000, from tiny villages to Paris. Citizens elect the conseil municipal, and the council elects the maire. The mairie handles the état civil (births, marriages, deaths), enrolment in public primary schools, local planning and, in many towns, the police municipale.

Communes often work together in an intercommunalité (communauté de communes, communauté d'agglomération or métropole). It usually runs services such as waste collection, water and local public transport. So the bin collection may depend on the intercommunalité and not on your mairie.

The conseil départemental handles social aid, child protection, services for older people and disabled people, collèges and departmental roads. The conseil régional handles lycées, regional trains (TER), economic development and vocational training. Teachers, the police nationale, the courts and tax offices stay with the State.

topics.title: Social security: branches, Urssaf and your payslip
topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on the public information of service-public.fr, securite-sociale.fr, ameli.fr, urssaf.fr and info-retraite.fr, as of 2026. Contribution rates, thresholds and amounts change every year and are deliberately left out. Check the official sites or ask the body concerned before you act.
topics.intro: The sécurité sociale is the public system behind health costs, family benefits, pensions and cover for accidents at work. You enter it by working or by living in France legally, and you get a numéro de sécurité sociale. This page explains the words you will meet on a payslip.
topics.question: Comment fonctionne la protection sociale dans ton pays ? (How does social protection work in your country?)
facts: The sécurité sociale has five risk branches: maladie, accidents du travail et maladies professionnelles, famille, retraite and autonomie (support for older people and for people with disabilities). The collection of contributions is handled separately, by the Urssaf.

Different bodies handle different branches. The CPAM (assurance maladie) deals with health care and the carte Vitale. The CAF pays family benefits and housing aid. For pensions, the Assurance retraite, often through the CARSAT, is responsible. The Urssaf collects contributions from employers and self-employed people.

Your numéro de sécurité sociale has 13 digits followed by a 2-digit key. When you start a job, the employer must send a DPAE (déclaration préalable à l'embauche) to the Urssaf before you begin. If you do not have a number yet, you get one through the assurance maladie: see the health-system page.

Cotisations sociales are contributions taken from pay. Some are paid by the employee (cotisations salariales, taken from the gross pay) and some by the employer (cotisations patronales). A contribution called the CSG also appears on payslips. This page gives no rates because they change: check urssaf.fr or ameli.fr.

On a fiche de paie (bulletin de salaire), read from top to bottom: the salaire brut, the list of cotisations, the net before income tax, the impôt prélevé à la source, and the net à payer, the amount that arrives in your bank account. Keep your payslips: many advisers say until retirement. Employers usually give them on paper or digitally.

Self-employed people (auto-entrepreneurs or micro-entrepreneurs) declare their chiffre d'affaires to the Urssaf and pay contributions as a percentage of it. For your pension, you can look at your relevé de carrière, the record of your trimestres, on the official site info-retraite.fr.

Registration deadlines, voting hours and rules for EU citizens are set before each election, so check service-public.fr before you act. This page describes the system and takes no position on parties or candidates.
topics.intro: In France you vote on Sundays, and for most elections in two rounds. Which elections you may vote in depends on your nationality. This page is a neutral overview of how the system works, not of the parties.
topics.question: Qui peut voter dans ton pays, et à quelles élections ? (Who may vote in your country, and in which elections?)
facts: The president of the Republic is elected by direct universal suffrage for five years, in two rounds. If nobody has an absolute majority in the first round, the two leading candidates go through to a second round two weeks later. The next presidential election is scheduled for spring 2027.

The Assemblée nationale has 577 députés, each elected in a circonscription for five years, also in two rounds. The Sénat is elected indirectly, by local elected officials. The president may dissolve the Assemblée nationale, which leads to new elections.

Municipal elections choose the conseillers municipaux for six years, and the council then elects the maire. Départementales and régionales choose the local councils. European elections choose France's members of the European Parliament every five years, in a single national vote.

Who may vote: French citizens aged 18 or over who are registered on the liste électorale and have not lost their civic rights. Young French citizens are normally registered automatically at 18. Otherwise you register at the mairie or online at service-public.fr, usually until about six weeks before the vote.

EU citizens living in France may vote in municipal and European elections if they register on a special list (liste électorale complémentaire). They cannot vote in presidential or legislative elections, and they cannot become mayor or deputy mayor. Citizens of other countries cannot vote in French elections, but naturalisation gives the right.

Before a vote, the mairie sends a carte électorale by post. On election day you go to your bureau de vote with an ID (pièce d'identité). Voting is not compulsory. If you cannot go, you can give a procuration to another voter, starting at maprocuration.gouv.fr. A vote blanc is counted separately from invalid votes.

topics.title: France and its former colonies
topics.sourceNote: General historical overview written neutrally. Dates are standard in history reference works and on vie-publique.fr, elysee.fr and diplomatie.gouv.fr (as of 2026). Historians, governments and families assess these events differently, and this page does not take a side.
topics.intro: France once ruled a large colonial empire in Africa, Asia, the Americas and the Pacific. This history still shapes language, migration and politics, and people judge it differently today. This page gives the main facts and shows where the debates are.
topics.question: Quelle date de l'histoire de ton pays est vue autrement dans d'autres pays ? (Which date in your country's history is seen differently in other countries?)
facts: The French colonial empire began in the 17th century in the Americas and grew mostly in the 19th and early 20th centuries in Africa, Southeast Asia and the Pacific. Slavery was abolished in the French colonies in 1848. A law of 2001 (the loi Taubira) recognises the slave trade and slavery as crimes against humanity, and 10 May is a national day of remembrance.

Algeria was conquered from 1830, and its northern territory was organised as French départements, with unequal rights for the settlers and for the Muslim population. The Algerian War lasted from 1954 to 1962. The Évian agreements were signed in March 1962 and Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962.

In Indochina (today Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia), the First Indochina War ran from 1946 to 1954 and ended after the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu and the Geneva agreements. In Africa, Morocco and Tunisia became independent in 1956. Guinea chose independence in 1958, and in 1960 many colonies, among them Senegal, Mali and Côte d'Ivoire, followed.

The word Françafrique describes the close political, economic and military ties that France kept with its former African colonies. Critics see lasting influence and interference. Supporters speak of cooperation, security and a shared language. In recent years France has reduced or ended its military presence in several countries, and the CFA franc is debated in a similar way.

Migration followed these links. After 1945 France recruited workers from Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia and West Africa, and families came in the 1970s. Today many people in France have roots in former colonies. Some overseas territories, such as Guadeloupe, Martinique and La Réunion, never left France and are part of it.

People disagree about how to judge colonisation. Some point to schools, hospitals and infrastructure, others to violence, inequality and forced labour, and historians work from the archives. Whether the State should issue an official apology, and how to teach this history, are questions of public debate.

topics.title: Historical memory: Vichy, Algeria and commemorations
topics.sourceNote: Dates and laws from legifrance.gouv.fr, vie-publique.fr, elysee.fr and the Ministère des Armées (memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr), as of 2026. How these periods should be judged and remembered is debated among historians, associations and politicians, and this page presents the debate without taking a side.
topics.intro: In France, history is not only taught: it is commemorated, debated and sometimes regulated by law. This page covers two painful periods, Vichy and the Algerian war, and the days on which the country remembers. It reports facts and debates and does not take a side.
topics.question: Comment se souvient-on, dans ton pays, d'une période difficile de l'histoire ? (How is a difficult period of history remembered in your country?)
facts: In June 1940, after the military defeat, France signed an armistice. A regime led by Marshal Pétain was set up in Vichy, and parliament gave him full powers on 10 July 1940. From October 1940 it passed anti-Jewish laws, and the French police and administration took part in arrests and deportations alongside the German occupiers.

The Vel' d'Hiv roundup took place in Paris on 16 and 17 July 1942. For decades, official speeches held that the Republic had ceased to exist under Vichy and was therefore not responsible. In 1995 President Chirac said that the French State had committed the irreparable. The two readings, the regime of the time and continuity of the State, are still discussed.

The Resistance and the Liberation are also remembered: General de Gaulle's appeal of 18 June 1940, the networks, the Liberation of 1944. In 1973 the historian Robert Paxton showed that Vichy's collaboration was also a policy of its own. Later work stressed that most people were neither heroes nor collaborators and that attitudes changed over time.

The Algerian war (1954 to 1962) was long called les événements in France, and a law of 1999 officially recognised the term guerre d'Algérie. Memory is divided between conscripts (appelés), pieds-noirs (Europeans who left Algeria in 1962), harkis (Algerians who served with the French army), Algerian families and victims of violence on all sides. The killing of Algerian demonstrators in Paris on 17 October 1961 has been the subject of official statements and continued discussion.

Dates themselves are debated. 19 March 1962 (the ceasefire) was made an official day of remembrance in 2012, but some associations of pieds-noirs and harkis reject it because the violence went on after that day. There is also a national day of tribute to the harkis on 25 September.

Two days are public holidays and are marked by ceremonies at the monument aux morts, usually with the mayor: 8 May (the end of the war in Europe in 1945) and 11 November (the armistice of 1918, and since 2012 a day for all who died for France). The lois mémorielles, which declare a historical fact by law, divide opinion: in 2005 many historians signed the appeal Liberté pour l'histoire, arguing that history should not be written by parliament, while others say that law can recognise victims.

topics.intro: The Constitution of the Fifth Republic, in force since 1958, is the highest text of French law. It sets out how the State works and refers to older texts on rights. The Conseil constitutionnel checks laws against it. This page is a neutral overview.
topics.question: Quels droits la constitution de ton pays garantit-elle ? (Which rights does your country's constitution guarantee?)
facts: The Constitution was approved by referendum on 28 September 1958 and promulgated on 4 October 1958, under General de Gaulle, which started the Fifth Republic. Since a referendum in 1962, the president has been elected directly. The text has been revised many times, for example in 2003 (decentralisation) and in 2008.

Its preamble refers to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789, to the preamble of the Constitution of 1946 and to the Charte de l'environnement of 2004. Together, these texts are called the bloc de constitutionnalité.

Article 1 says: « La France est une République indivisible, laïque, démocratique et sociale. » The motto is Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité, the flag is the tricolore, the anthem is La Marseillaise, and French is the language of the Republic (article 2). Marianne, a woman with a Phrygian cap, is the symbol of the Republic, and her bust is in many mairies.

Laïcité rests on the law of 9 December 1905, which separated the Churches and the State. The State is neutral, guarantees freedom of conscience and worship, and does not recognise, pay or subsidise any religion (with a historical exception in Alsace-Moselle). A law of 2004 bans conspicuous religious signs in public schools. Its meaning is debated: some stress the protection of freedom of belief, others worry that it limits some believers.

The Conseil constitutionnel sits at the Palais-Royal in Paris. It has nine members, appointed for nine years without renewal: the president of the Republic, the president of the Assemblée nationale and the president of the Sénat each name three. Former presidents of the Republic may also sit by right.

It can check a law before it comes into force when asked by the president, the Prime Minister, the presidents of the two chambers, or 60 députés or 60 sénateurs. Since 2010 any person in a trial can raise a QPC (question prioritaire de constitutionnalité), which reaches the Council through the courts. The Council also supervises presidential and parliamentary elections and referendums.

topics.title: Unions, collective agreements and workers' rights
topics.sourceNote: Preamble of the Constitution of 1946, the Code du travail (legifrance.gouv.fr) and the public guides of service-public.fr, travail-emploi.gouv.fr and code.travail.gouv.fr, as of 2026. General orientation, not legal advice. Thresholds and deadlines depend on your situation and change, so check the Code du travail numérique or ask a union, the inspection du travail or a lawyer.
topics.intro: In France, the basic rules at work come from the Code du travail, from the convention collective of your sector and from your contract. Unions and elected staff representatives help to apply them. Joining a union is voluntary. This is general information, not legal advice.
topics.question: Quel rôle ont les syndicats dans ton pays ? (What role do unions have in your country?)
facts: The preamble of the Constitution of 1946, which is still part of French constitutional law, recognises the right to strike, the freedom to join a union, and the right of workers to take part in decisions through their representatives. The Code du travail is the main labour law. A contract or an agreement can improve on it but normally cannot go below it.

A convention collective covers a whole sector, such as restaurants, construction or retail. It sets things like minimum pay grids and extra leave. It usually applies to your employer because of the sector, whether or not you are a union member. Your payslip should show the name of the convention that applies.

The main union confederations include the CGT, the CFDT, Force ouvrière (FO), the CFE-CGC and the CFTC, along with others such as the UNSA and Solidaires. Joining is voluntary, and only part of the employees are members. Unions can negotiate agreements, advise employees and support them in a dispute.

In companies with at least 11 employees, there is a CSE (comité social et économique), elected by the staff. It receives information on the company, passes on employees' questions and, in larger companies, has more powers, including on health and safety. In very small companies there is no CSE, so ask your employer, a union or the inspection du travail.

Strike is a recognised right. In the private sector each employee decides for themselves. Strike days are normally unpaid, and in some public services a notice (préavis) is required. Rules are detailed, so ask a union or check service-public.fr before taking part.

The conseil de prud'hommes is the labour court for disputes between an employee and an employer, for instance about a contract or a dismissal. It has elected employee and employer judges and starts with an attempt at conciliation. Deadlines are short, so act early. The inspection du travail is a State service that checks that the Code du travail is respected and that you can contact with questions or complaints.
